docs.text: What Archi is Archi automates operations for scientific computing: experiment computing operations, analysis user support, data quality and cluster management. Agents watch the system and propose actions. Once a person approves a proposal, a separate component carries it out; in 3.0 no automation acts on its own. Every step is grounded in your facility's own knowledge, and its result is written back into that knowledge. Archi 3.0 ships the context layer, the automation runtime and two automations. ticket-triage triages new and updated Redmine, JIRA and ServiceNow tickets: it drafts a cited reply for a person to send, or proposes a status change, assignment or reply that runs only after a person approves it. instance-health watches the Archi instance itself. Archi is built on OKG, a knowledge graph with a publish step, a set of read tools and a review ledger. You do not need to know OKG to start. This site explains each OKG idea where Archi uses it. Note This is the 3.0 documentation. The earlier chatbot is documented under v2 (legacy) . See Moving from v2 to 3.0 . Two layers Automation is only as good as what the agent knows. So Archi has two layers. The context layer holds what your facility knows: documentation, tickets, catalogs, monitoring, code and the record of past operations. It has to be solid. That means current, complete for the questions automations depend on, linked across sources, cited on every read, and measured. The operations layer runs automations over that context. Each one follows the same loop: signal, context, proposal, decision, action, outcome. Actions run under explicit autonomy levels, up to L2 in 3.0. Outcomes go back into the context layer, so the next triage can see what happened last time. The working rule is: algorithmic first, agents for judgment. Fixed checks (invariants, freshness, thresholds, evals) decide everything they can. Agents handle what needs reading and judgment. What you install You install a bundle : a named selection of packs. A pack is the smallest installable piece, such as one source family or one automation. Four bundles ship today: Bundle For cern-team Any CERN team: documentation and meetings, with no credentials needed to start. cms-physics CMS physics: analysis notes, published summaries, physics TWiki pages and the analyses that link them. cms-comp-ops CMS computing operations: sites, storage, datasets, workflows, site status and past incidents. cluster-manager Any cluster operator, at any site: documentation, tickets, operational memory, and optionally Slurm, HTCondor, ServiceNow and node health. The library lists every bundle and pack with what it reads. Your own sources and automations can ship as packs from your own package. Start with the quickstart : it takes an empty machine to a cited answer with the cern-team bundle. Parts you can replace Most parts can be replaced, and the defaults work out of the box. The knowledge graph and the automation runtime cannot be replaced in 3.0. Part Default in 3.0 How you replace it Knowledge graph OKG (AKMON) Not replaceable in 3.0. The MCP tool surface ( search , expand , inspect , filter , map , aggregate ) is the contract another store would have to meet. Ingestion Archi connectors Any pip package that registers packs through the archi.packs entry point. See Contributing a pack . Tools The instance's OKG MCP server plus Archi live tools Any MCP server declared in the instance. See Connecting an agent . Automation runtime OKG deployment workflows An external runner using the proposal API. This waits on an upstream OKG change. Agent and chat Open WebUI, built in Anything that speaks MCP: Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw, your own. Language model Chat: a local ollama model (default llama3.1:8b ). Agents over MCP: the agent's own model. Chat: --answer chat_model= , --ollama-url , or a connection added in Open WebUI. Agents: their own configuration. Archi stores no model API key. Who it is for First, operations teams: CMS computing operations, CRAB support, WisDQM and cluster managers at any site. Second, a team that only wants the context layer and an agent over it in an afternoon. That team installs the same bundles with no automation selected. The design is in ADR 0002 .

docs.text: Adding a source A source is one connector reading one system into the graph. Sources come inside context packs, so adding a source means adding a pack. Add a shipped pack Find the pack in the library . Its page lists the questions it asks and the credential names it reads. Add it to the running instance: bash archi add git-code --answer git_code_repo_url=https://github.com/example/repo.git --answer ID=VALUE answers one of the pack's questions. The id is the pack name, with dashes as underscores, then an underscore and the question id. archi add edits the registry, claims ownership of the new source, commits the instance repository, and publishes again. 3. Run archi doctor . The source-freshness check shows the new source's age against its limit. To choose packs at the start, use archi init --with <pack> . Credentials A pack names its credential variables (its page lists them). It never holds a value. Packs that need no credential, such as docsite , publish with nothing configured. Where the value goes. Put it in the instance's .env , one KEY=value per line, or in a cookie file whose path an init question asks for. .env is mode 0600 and git ignores it. Quotes around a value and a leading export are allowed. What reads it. archi add , archi ingest and every other okg command archi runs add every value in .env to the environment of the steps that ingest. A value exported in the shell wins. A value added to .env takes effect at the next archi ingest or archi add . Keys that change how programs run ( PATH , LD_* , PYTHON* , GIT_* , SSH_* , OKG_* ) are not passed on; archi names them on stderr. What does not read it. okg run by hand. To refresh sources, run archi ingest instead ( --include <source id>,... for some of them, --publish to publish after). The first ingest of archi init , because archi init writes .env itself. For a pack selected at archi init , export the value in the shell, then add it to .env . The ops runtime worker, which you start yourself. Start it from a shell that has the credentials exported. Connectors that read a cache Some connectors read a cache that another tool writes, for example the CRIC topology or the DBS dataset catalog. Each cache has a contract: where it lives and what it holds. See connector caches . A pack's prepare: step can write a cache before the first run, so a bare install has its input. A source Archi does not ship Write a pack. A pack can live in another pip package and register through the archi.packs entry point. See Contributing a pack .

docs.text: Bundles and packs Packs A pack is the smallest installable capability. There are three kinds: context packs bring sources: one family of documents, tickets, catalogs or code tool packs bring live tools: functions an agent can call over MCP automation packs bring one automation (see the operations layer ) A pack is a directory with a pack.yaml and the files it names: schemas, source templates, init questions, invariants, playbooks. It owns its invariants and freshness limits, so removing the pack removes them too. A pack that is not selected leaves no trace in the instance. Bundles A bundle is a named, versioned selection of packs, plus a chat preset. It lists default packs (installed unless you remove them) and optional packs (installed when you ask). A bundle can extend others and inherits their defaults. A bundle also sets the highest autonomy level for any automation it selects. It never sets the level itself. Bundle Purpose cern-team A generic CERN team knowledge instance: documentation, meetings, wiki, documents, tickets and code. No automations. cms-physics A CMS physics knowledge instance. Extends cern-team . cms-comp-ops A CMS computing operations instance: CMS catalogs, site status, CMSSW releases and the operational memory. Extends cern-team . Optional: monit-live , dqm , hypernews , jira , ticket-triage . cluster-manager A knowledge instance for people who run a batch cluster: documentation, Redmine tickets and operational memory, with optional ServiceNow, Slurm, HTCondor, node health and code. It depends on no CERN pack. Its Slurm pack ships live tools whose actions (drain or resume a node, requeue a job) run only after an approved escalation. The optional ticket-triage automation drafts a cited triage note for each new or updated ticket. See the bundle README . The library has one generated page per bundle and per pack, so it matches what ships. Choosing packs archi init myteam --bundle cern-team --with git-code,jira --without indico archi bundles list archi bundles show cern-team The result is the closure of what the packs require, plus the defaults of the selected bundles, plus --with , minus --without . Several bundles can go into one instance by repeating --bundle . The rendered profile and an archi.lock (bundle and pack versions plus content digests) are committed into the instance repository. Two properties always hold: A bundle with nothing configured publishes. Each bundle has at least one default context pack that needs no credential, or a required question. A pack that is not selected does not appear in the rendered profile. archi add <pack> adds a pack to a running instance and publishes again. archi diff shows how the instance has drifted from its lock. More Library : every bundle and pack in this release. Pack and bundle format : every key in pack.yaml and bundle.yaml , and the composition rules. Contributing a pack .

docs.text: Connecting other agents ( archi connect ) Open WebUI is one client of an instance. Any agent that speaks MCP over streamable HTTP can use the same graph tools. The endpoint is http://127.0.0.1:<ports.mcp>/mcp ; the bearer token is OKG_CHAT_MCP_TOKEN in the instance .env . Who can read the graph In 3.0, access is all or nothing. Every client of an instance uses the same token, and anyone who holds it can read the whole published graph. There is no per-user, per-group or per-record filtering, and no single sign-on for the MCP endpoint. A request with no token or a wrong one gets HTTP 401. Clients connected with archi connect also get query , the raw SQL read tool. The Open WebUI preset leaves it out, but the server offers it to every client that holds the token. It runs as the read-only okg_mcp database role and refuses anything but SELECT and WITH . Give the token only to people who may read everything in the instance. The ports listen on 127.0.0.1 only. To reach the instance from another machine, use an SSH tunnel. Configure a client archi connect claude-code [--instance DIR] [--print | --write [PATH]] [--show-token] [--embed-token] --print (the default) shows the config. --write merges it into the client's config file (default path below). A config file that exists is never replaced: archi adds or updates its own entries ( archi-<instance name> and the external servers) and keeps everything else. Running the same command again changes nothing. A file that archi cannot parse is left alone and the command stops. The token is not printed unless you pass --show-token . Printed and written configs carry ${OKG_CHAT_MCP_TOKEN} , which Claude Code and OpenClaw expand from the environment, so export the variable (from the instance .env ) in the shell that starts the client. A new file is mode 0600. --write --embed-token writes the literal token instead; archi refuses unless the file is outside any git repository or git ignores it ( git check-ignore ), and tightens an existing file to 0600. A symlinked config is written through to its target. For Codex, archi sets only the keys it owns in [mcp_servers.<name>] ( url , bearer_token_env_var , env_http_headers ). Your own keys there ( startup_timeout_sec , tool_timeout_sec , enabled , sub-tables) and the rest of the file are kept. The file is read with a TOML parser, and the result is checked to differ from the old file only in those tables; otherwise nothing is written. Client Default file Format Checked how claude-code ./.mcp.json mcpServers.<name> with type: "http" , url , headers Matches what claude mcp add --transport http NAME URL --header "H: V" writes (run against the installed CLI). codex ~/.codex/config.toml [mcp_servers.<name>] with url , bearer_token_env_var , env_http_headers Codex's MCP documentation. Codex speaks streamable HTTP itself; no stdio bridge such as mcp-remote is needed. Codex reads the token from the environment: export OKG_CHAT_MCP_TOKEN=... . Not run against a Codex binary. openclaw ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json mcp.servers.<name> with url , transport: "streamable-http" , headers OpenClaw's configuration documentation only; not run against a live OpenClaw . The file is JSON5: archi merges only strict JSON and otherwise tells you to merge by hand. Check with openclaw mcp show . mcp ./archi-mcp.json mcpServers.<name> JSON The shape most MCP clients read; for any client not listed. open-webui none none archi up already registered the server ( okg chat sync ); the command prints the URL the site uses ( http://mcp:<port>/mcp ), the site URL and where the token is. External MCP servers Declare them in the instance's archi.yaml : mcp_servers: - name: notes # lowercase letters, digits, - _ url: https://notes.example.org/mcp headers: Authorization: NOTES_AUTH # header name -> NAME of an environment variable The variable holds the whole header value (for example Bearer abc ). The file is committed, so it never holds a secret; a value that is not a variable name, a URL with credentials or a query string, an unknown key, a duplicate name or the instance's own server name stops archi connect with the reason. archi connect writes these entries next to the instance's own, as ${NOTES_AUTH} references (Codex: env_http_headers ). Export the variable before starting the client. Open WebUI is not synced from this block; the command lists them to add under Settings > Admin > External Tools. Checking a recipe without a model python/tests/connect/recipe_check.py reads a written config, connects exactly as the client would (URL and headers as written; ${VAR} and Codex's variables come from the environment or --env-file DIR/.env ; an unset variable is an error), calls search on the instance server and echo on any external server that has one, and prints a JSON result. Exit 0 means every call succeeded. archi connect claude-code --write /tmp/probe/.mcp.json python python/tests/connect/recipe_check.py --client claude-code \ --config /tmp/probe/.mcp.json --env-file DIR/.env --query "CMSSW" For Open WebUI, python/tests/connect/webui_check.py --instance DIR signs in as the site admin, reads the tool server the site registered, and runs an MCP client inside the webui container ( podman|docker exec ) that calls search at that registered URL over the compose network; it exits 0 only if the answer cites rows. python/tests/connect/fixtures/echo_server.py is a small external server (one echo tool) for trying the mcp_servers: path.

docs.text: The context layer The context layer is the knowledge graph plus the checks that say whether you can trust it. Automations act on what it says, so "solid" has to be measured and checked by machine. It is never just asserted. What "solid" means Property What it means How it is checked Status in this branch Current Each source is recent enough. Each pack declares max_staleness for each source. OKG records when each source last finished a run. archi doctor compares the two. Working Complete The graph holds what each pack should emit. Each pack owns coverage invariants. A failing error invariant blocks the publish. Working Linked Identifiers (sites, datasets, runs, releases, tickets) connect records across sources. Each pack can declare link coverage targets. Working Cited Every answer and every proposal names the records it used. OKG reads are pinned to one published generation. A proposal must list evidence ids. Working Measured Operator questions with known right evidence are scored. Context evals ( archi eval --context ). Working; each instance keeps its own question set Clean No credentials or personal data in the graph. Redaction at ingest, connector tests. Working in the connectors A generation is one published snapshot of the graph. An invariant is a stored query that must return no rows. A publish makes a new generation visible to readers. Freshness A pack that has sources lists a freshness limit for each one: freshness: indico.indico_live: {max_staleness: 24h} The unit is s , m , h , d or w . The value is a judgment: how old the source may get before an answer from it is probably wrong. archi doctor reads each source's last completed run from OKG and reports it late when the age passes the limit, or when OKG lists no run at all. See Context quality for the JSON it prints. Link coverage A pack that carries identifiers other packs refer to declares how well they must link. For example, "at least 90% of storage endpoints sit under a site". Archi turns each target into an invariant named <pack>_link_<name> . A miss is a warning by default. Set severity: error where a miss should block the publish. The library pages list each pack's targets, for example cms-catalogs . The context gate An automation says which context it needs: sources, a maximum staleness, a minimum context-eval score (with max_age_days , default 14, context_eval_bundle when the instance has more than one bundle, and the optional pins context_eval_k and context_eval_min_questions ) and the invariants that must hold. Before each run the runtime checks that gate against the current generation. If any check fails, the run drops to shadow mode: it proposes and records, and never acts. The proposal names the failing check, so the operator sees why. Failing checks are named freshness:<source> , context_eval , invariant:<name> and published . A missing score or result counts as a failure. An automation that watches the instance itself asks only for published . It has to keep running while a source is stale. Context evals A context eval is a set of operator questions, each with the evidence that should answer it (its gold node ids). archi eval --context scores retrieval (was the right evidence found) separately from answer quality: it calls the instance's MCP search tool directly, with no model, and reports recall@k of the gold ids for the graph search and for a lexical baseline (the server's lexical index over chunks and attributes, without roll-up to records). The graph search is lexical too, with concept expansion and record roll-up on, so the difference measures those, not graph links. Each run is kept under <data root>/eval/context/<bundle>/<UTC stamp>/ . The graph search's recall@k is the score: the context gate reads the newest run of its bundle for min_context_eval_score , and fails the check, naming the reason, when there is none, or it cannot be read, did not execute cleanly, overrode the graph arm, is older than max_age_days (default 14) or dated in the future, or misses the gate's optional context_eval_k and context_eval_min_questions pins. The instance-health automation does not read context evals. Question sets are private to the instance and never committed here; name one at run time with --questions or ARCHI_CONTEXT_EVAL_QUESTIONS . See Operating . ops-record: the operational memory The ops-record pack stores the record of operations in the graph, next to the docs and tickets it cites: incident: what broke, where, when proposal: what an automation suggested, and on which evidence decision: who or what approved or rejected it, and when action: what the mediator ran, and what it returned outcome: whether it worked, checked later Automations write these records through OKG admission, the same path any producer uses. Past resolutions then become context ("this transfer error last time was fixed by..."). The record also serves as the test set for the next automation. See the ops-record page .
docs.title: The context layer

docs.text: Contributing a pack from your own package An external group can ship packs, bundles and connectors as an ordinary Python package. Nothing lands in the archi repository. ADR 0002 section 4.4 is the design; Pack and bundle format is the reference for the manifest files. This page says what your package must contain and how to test it. What the package declares Entry points. One per directory you ship: toml [project.entry-points."archi.packs"] mywg = "mywg_packs:packs_dir" # returns a directory of <pack>/pack.yaml [project.entry-points."archi.bundles"] mywg = "mywg_packs:bundles_dir" # optional: a directory of <bundle>/bundle.yaml The value is a callable returning the directory (or the directory itself). The entry-point name ( mywg ) is the provider label users see. Pack manifests , one packs/<name>/pack.yaml each, valid against the published schema ( archi bundles validate <dir> ). Package the directories as data files in your wheel. Rules that bite external packs: pack names are global: two providers with the same name are both reported as a problem, so prefix yours ( mywg-... ); a pack that needs a credential sets needs_credentials: true and names environment variables in credentials ; never a value; every context-pack source has a freshness entry; automation packs cannot ask for a level above L2. Connectors. A connector is the code that pulls one external system into the graph. It is an okg SourceAdapter (okg's mechanism name), referenced from a source template in the pack by module: and class: : yaml mywg-tickets: module: mywg_connectors.tickets class: TicketSource ownership_id: ${deployment_name}.mywg-tickets admission_policy: { ... } # producer authority, output_signature, as okg requires Your package must be importable in the environment where okg runs, so list okg as an install-time requirement of the deployment, not of your wheel (okg is the host environment; archi does not declare it either). The adapter contract (change probes, producer authority, admission mode, record identity) is okg's, and okg alignment lists the interface archi relies on. Versioning Each pack and bundle has its own version ( MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH ). Raise MAJOR when a source's output signature, record identity or a question id changes: an instance's archi.lock records the selection and archi diff reports drift. Each bundle states the okg range it supports in okg: (PEP 440, for example ">=0.6.0,<0.7" ). A pack inherits the check through the bundles that use it. The wheel's version is yours. Pin the range of archi-kb you were tested against in your own dependencies . What users see With your wheel installed in the same environment as archi: $ archi bundles list ... mywg-tickets 0.1.0 (context, needs credentials) [mywg (mywg-packs 0.1.0)] The bracket is the provider: the entry-point name and the distribution and version that registered it. archi bundles list --json has it as provider . Use archi render --bundle B --with mywg-tickets --instance DIR or archi add mywg-tickets --instance DIR to install it. How to test it archi bundles validate path/to/packs must report no problem. archi bundles list --json must show your packs with your provider label and an empty problems list. A broken entry point is listed, not fatal. archi render --bundle <your bundle> --instance <tmp> then okg install --profile <name> --dry-run --json --non-interactive ... must report dry_run_ok with no blockers. Publish against a real graph database in your own CI, the way archi init does. archi's own copy of steps 2 and 3 runs against a fixture package, python/tests/bundles/fixtures/thirdparty/archi_fixture_packs/ , built into a wheel in python/tests/bundles/test_packaging.py . Copy that package as a starting point. Bringing an MCP server instead If what you have is a live tool and not ingestion, you do not need a pack: declare it under mcp_servers: in the instance's archi.yaml and archi connect registers it next to the instance server ( Connecting other agents ).

docs.text: Moving from v2 to 3.0 Short version. 3.0 is a new install, not an upgrade. You do not convert a v2 config file or a v2 database. You back v2 up, start a 3.0 instance beside it, point the new instance at the same sources, compare answers, and move your users when you are satisfied. v2 keeps running the whole time, and you can stop at any step and lose nothing. This page is for an operator who runs a v2 deployment from the main branch ( archi create ... ). The date the v3 line becomes main is the cutover . Until then main receives only v2 bug fixes. After it, v2 lives on the v2 branch with its v2.x tags, and nothing in a running v2 deployment changes by itself. The v2 documentation stays on this site under v2 (legacy) . What changes In v2 In 3.0 A RAG chatbot you configure with one large YAML file and deploy with archi create . A knowledge graph you install from a bundle with archi init and archi up . Settings live in archi.yaml and in the packs. Documents are chunked into a vector store the app owns. OKG owns retrieval. Every answer cites records from one published generation. The chat app, uploader and data viewer are Archi's own web apps. Open WebUI is one built-in client. Any MCP client can read the graph. See Connecting an agent . You pick a model provider (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, local) in the Archi config. Archi stores no model. The agent is configured with its own. Sources are listed under data_manager.sources (links, git, Indico, JIRA, Redmine). Sources come in packs: docsite , indico , jira , tickets (Redmine and JIRA), git-code and more. See the library . Queue bots (Redmine, JIRA, Mattermost) draft replies. Automations under autonomy levels, with a shadow period before going live. See the operations layer . Quality is checked with archi evaluate (Ragas benchmark). archi eval (smoke sets with deterministic checks) and archi eval --context (retrieval scored against gold evidence). See archi eval . Redeploy with archi restart . archi up , archi down , archi add , archi diff . See Operating . What has no equivalent yet Check this list before you plan a move. Each item is a v2 feature that 3.0.0 does not have. Resolution emails and mail intake. At SubMIT, ticket-triage replaces the v2 Redmine bot at the cutover, with no shadow trial first (board d717). The v2 service that posted the bot's answers also sent the resolution email, and it stops at the cutover, so SubMIT users get no resolution emails from the cutover until 3.1 (board d719). The repository owner tells the SubMIT A2rchi owner and the SubMIT users before the cutover. Mail intake (emails turned into tickets) stays on v2 until 3.1 (board d704). The other v2 bots (JIRA ticket responder, Mattermost) keep serving on a tagged v2.x . The Ragas benchmark. archi evaluate scored answers with an LLM judge. archi eval replaces it with deterministic checks (cited records and required strings) and a retrieval score; there is no LLM-judged score. The Piazza bot. It is retired and will not be ported. The grader app, the A/B tools and the playbook store. The design drops them. The v2.x tags keep them. Document upload through the chat UI, and files copied into the data folder. There is no upload source. To get a document in, publish it somewhere a pack reads (a documentation site, a Git repository) or write a pack. The service status board and alert banners. Not ported. Web pages behind a login ( sso- links). The docsite pack reads public pages only. hypernews reads an SSO cookie file, which is interactive to make. There is no general SSO page scraper. More than one Git repository per git-code pack, and the v2 "MkDocs repository" mode. git-code reads one repository's tracked files and history. Restricted Indico events. The indico pack reads public events and asks for no credential. Helm deployment. 3.0 runs one compose project with podman or docker. SSO login and admin roles for the chat ( services.chat_app.auth , auth_roles ). Open WebUI keeps its own accounts, but every chat user and every connected agent reads the graph through one shared token, with no per-user or per-role filtering. See who can read the graph . Live instances rebuilt from the bundles. All four bundles ship ( cern-team , cms-physics , cms-comp-ops , cluster-manager ), but the live comp-ops and SubMIT instances have not been rebuilt from them yet. Before you start: back up v2 Nothing here changes v2. Do it once, before anything else, and keep the backup until you have retired the v2 deployment. v2 keeps three things you care about: the deployment folder , ~/.archi/archi-<name> (or $ARCHI_DIR/archi-<name> ): the rendered compose file, your config and the secrets; the Postgres volume archi-pg-<name> : conversations, document records, and the data manager's catalog; the data volume archi-data-<name> : the scraped and uploaded documents. Set RT to docker or podman , whichever v2 runs on, and NAME to the deployment name that archi list-deployments prints. RT=docker # or podman NAME=my-archi BK=~/archi-v2-backup/$NAME && mkdir -p "$BK" && cd "$BK" archi list-deployments # confirm the name cp -a ~/.archi/archi-$NAME ./deployment # config, compose file, secrets $RT exec postgres-$NAME pg_dump -U archi -d archi-db -Fc > archi-db.dump $RT run --rm -v archi-data-$NAME:/data -v "$PWD":/backup alpine \ tar czf /backup/archi-data.tgz -C /data . ls -l # three non-empty items Checks: archi-db.dump is not empty, and pg_restore --list archi-db.dump | head (if you have pg_restore on the host) prints a table of contents. archi-data.tgz lists with tar tzf archi-data.tgz | head . The deployment folder holds secrets, so keep the backup folder private. Write down which v2 sources and services you run: the data_manager.sources block of your config, and the --services you passed to archi create . You need them in the next sections. Stand up 3.0 beside v2 Use a new Python environment. The v2 and 3.0 command-line programs are both called archi . Do not install 3.0 into the environment that runs v2. bash python3 -m venv ~/archi3-venv . ~/archi3-venv/bin/activate pip install archi-kb==3.0.2 archi --help Check that archi --help lists init and up . If it lists create , you are still in the v2 environment. Make the instance under another name. Pick a name that v2 does not use (here NAME3 ). Ports are chosen free at init time and bound to 127.0.0.1, so they do not collide with v2. The instance lives in its own directory and its own containers and volumes. The 3.0 name takes lowercase letters, digits and - only (no _ , no capitals), so pick another NAME3 if your v2 name has either. bash NAME3=${NAME}-v3 archi init $NAME3 --bundle cern-team --dir ~/archi3/$NAME3 cd ~/archi3/$NAME3 archi up archi doctor archi doctor exits 0 when no check failed. archi up prints the chat address and the MCP endpoint. Add your sources (next section), then run archi doctor again. Its source-freshness check shows each source's age against its limit. Ask your real questions. Use the questions your users ask v2, in the chat or through an agent . Compare the cited answers with v2's. Record which questions are worse and why. Move your users when 3.0 answers well and nothing in the list above blocks you. Keep v2 running as long as you need. Move each source archi init --with <pack> chooses packs at the start. archi add <pack> adds one to a running instance and publishes again. --answer ID=VALUE answers one of the pack's questions; the id is the pack name with dashes as underscores, then _ and the question id. Credentials never go on the command line: put the value in .env in the instance, under the name the pack lists. v2 source 3.0 pack How to move it links : public web pages from .list files docsite archi add docsite --answer docsite_urls=<url>[,<url>...] . Give the documentation sites or pages to read. It downloads the pages first, then ingests. A page that cannot be fetched stops the add before it edits anything. links behind SSO ( sso- prefix) none No equivalent. Leave these on v2 or publish the content where a pack can read it. git (an MkDocs repository, git- prefix) git-code archi add git-code --answer git_code_repo_url=<url> --answer git_code_repo_name=<short name> . It reads every tracked file and the history, not only the Markdown. One repository per instance. indico indico archi add indico --answer indico_event_ids='["<id>"]' or --answer indico_category_ids='["<id>"]' . Public events only. With no answer it reads the CERN workshop event 1716863. jira jira Archi reads a cache that a downloader writes, and archi add jira stops if the cache is missing. So download first: python -m archi.downloaders.jira --output-dir <data root>/jira --project <KEY> (repeat --project ; set CERN_JIRA_TOKEN in the environment if the projects are not public), then archi add jira . <data root> is the data_root: value in archi.yaml . The downloader needs the jira Python package ( pip install jira ). See python -m archi.downloaders.jira --help . Refreshing the cache is yours to schedule: the pack expects data no older than 24 hours, and archi doctor reports it when it is older. redmine tickets Like jira , Archi reads a cache that a downloader writes. Download first: python -m archi.downloaders.tickets --output-dir <data root>/tickets --redmine-url <url> (set REDMINE_API_KEY in the environment), then archi add tickets --answer tickets_base_url=<url> . The same pack reads JIRA Server or Data Center with --jira-url . See python -m archi.downloaders.tickets --help . Uploaded files, files copied into the data folder none No equivalent. Mattermost, Piazza, grader, Grafana service board none Not ported. See above. Adding a source says more about packs, and connector caches says what each downloader writes. The library lists every pack with its questions and credentials. Roll back Each stage has its own way back. v2 is never edited by the move, so the first two cost nothing. Abandon the 3.0 instance. v2 is untouched. From the instance directory: bash archi down --purge --yes # stops the stack and deletes its volumes cd ~ && rm -rf ~/archi3/$NAME3 Delete ~/.local/share/archi/$NAME3 too if you want the connector caches gone (that is the default data root). Pause a move. Run archi down (no --purge ). It keeps every volume. archi up brings the instance back with the same graph. Return your users to v2. If you pointed users or a proxy at 3.0, point them back. v2 never stopped. Restore v2 itself (only if v2 was damaged, for example after the cutover moved its branch). Use the v2 line, not 3.0. In a v2 environment: bash git checkout v2.5.0 # or the newest v2.x tag your site pinned pip install -e . archi delete -n $NAME # only if a broken deployment is still there archi create -n $NAME -c "$BK/deployment/<your config>.yaml" \ -e "$BK/deployment/<your secrets>.env" --services <your services> $RT exec -i postgres-$NAME pg_restore -U archi -d archi-db --clean --if-exists < "$BK/archi-db.dump" $RT run --rm -v archi-data-$NAME:/data -v "$BK":/backup alpine \ tar xzf /backup/archi-data.tgz -C /data The config and secrets are the files you used the first time. The copy of the deployment folder in the backup shows which they were. archi delete without --rmv keeps the volumes, and the restore then overwrites them. Tell the maintainers If you run a v2 deployment, tell the maintainers. The cutover waits until every live deployment has a named owner and has either moved or chosen to stay on a tagged v2.x release. A deployment that stays on v2 should pin the tag it runs, so a later fix on main cannot change it.

The Piazza bot. It is retired and will not be ported. The grader app, the A/B tools and the playbook store. The design drops them. The v2.x tags keep them. Document upload through the chat UI, and files copied into the data folder. There is no upload source. To get a document in, publish it somewhere a pack reads (a documentation site, a Git repository) or write a pack. The service status board and alert banners. Not ported. Web pages behind a login ( sso- links). The docsite pack reads public pages only. hypernews reads an SSO cookie file, which is interactive to make. There is no general SSO page scraper. More than one Git repository per git-code pack, and the v2 "MkDocs repository" mode. git-code reads one repository's tracked files and history. Restricted Indico events. The indico pack reads public events and asks for no credential. Helm deployment. 3.0 runs one compose project with podman or docker. SSO login and admin roles for the chat ( services.chat_app.auth , auth_roles ). Open WebUI keeps its own accounts, but every chat user and every connected agent reads the graph through one shared token, with no per-user or per-role filtering. See who can read the graph . Live instances rebuilt from the bundles. All four bundles ship ( cern-team , cms-physics , cms-comp-ops , cluster-manager ), but the live comp-ops and SubMIT instances have not been rebuilt from them yet.
docs.title: What has no equivalent yet

docs.text: Nothing here changes v2. Do it once, before anything else, and keep the backup until you have retired the v2 deployment. v2 keeps three things you care about: the deployment folder , ~/.archi/archi-<name> (or $ARCHI_DIR/archi-<name> ): the rendered compose file, your config and the secrets; the Postgres volume archi-pg-<name> : conversations, document records, and the data manager's catalog; the data volume archi-data-<name> : the scraped and uploaded documents. Set RT to docker or podman , whichever v2 runs on, and NAME to the deployment name that archi list-deployments prints. RT=docker # or podman NAME=my-archi BK=~/archi-v2-backup/$NAME && mkdir -p "$BK" && cd "$BK" archi list-deployments # confirm the name cp -a ~/.archi/archi-$NAME ./deployment # config, compose file, secrets $RT exec postgres-$NAME pg_dump -U archi -d archi-db -Fc > archi-db.dump $RT run --rm -v archi-data-$NAME:/data -v "$PWD":/backup alpine \ tar czf /backup/archi-data.tgz -C /data . ls -l # three non-empty items Checks: archi-db.dump is not empty, and pg_restore --list archi-db.dump | head (if you have pg_restore on the host) prints a table of contents. archi-data.tgz lists with tar tzf archi-data.tgz | head . The deployment folder holds secrets, so keep the backup folder private. Write down which v2 sources and services you run: the data_manager.sources block of your config, and the --services you passed to archi create . You need them in the next sections.
docs.title: Before you start: back up v2

docs.text: Use a new Python environment. The v2 and 3.0 command-line programs are both called archi . Do not install 3.0 into the environment that runs v2. bash python3 -m venv ~/archi3-venv . ~/archi3-venv/bin/activate pip install archi-kb==3.0.2 archi --help Check that archi --help lists init and up . If it lists create , you are still in the v2 environment. Make the instance under another name. Pick a name that v2 does not use (here NAME3 ). Ports are chosen free at init time and bound to 127.0.0.1, so they do not collide with v2. The instance lives in its own directory and its own containers and volumes. The 3.0 name takes lowercase letters, digits and - only (no _ , no capitals), so pick another NAME3 if your v2 name has either. bash NAME3=${NAME}-v3 archi init $NAME3 --bundle cern-team --dir ~/archi3/$NAME3 cd ~/archi3/$NAME3 archi up archi doctor archi doctor exits 0 when no check failed. archi up prints the chat address and the MCP endpoint. Add your sources (next section), then run archi doctor again. Its source-freshness check shows each source's age against its limit. Ask your real questions. Use the questions your users ask v2, in the chat or through an agent . Compare the cited answers with v2's. Record which questions are worse and why. Move your users when 3.0 answers well and nothing in the list above blocks you. Keep v2 running as long as you need.
docs.title: Stand up 3.0 beside v2

docs.text: archi init --with <pack> chooses packs at the start. archi add <pack> adds one to a running instance and publishes again. --answer ID=VALUE answers one of the pack's questions; the id is the pack name with dashes as underscores, then _ and the question id. Credentials never go on the command line: put the value in .env in the instance, under the name the pack lists. v2 source 3.0 pack How to move it links : public web pages from .list files docsite archi add docsite --answer docsite_urls=<url>[,<url>...] . Give the documentation sites or pages to read. It downloads the pages first, then ingests. A page that cannot be fetched stops the add before it edits anything. links behind SSO ( sso- prefix) none No equivalent. Leave these on v2 or publish the content where a pack can read it. git (an MkDocs repository, git- prefix) git-code archi add git-code --answer git_code_repo_url=<url> --answer git_code_repo_name=<short name> . It reads every tracked file and the history, not only the Markdown. One repository per instance. indico indico archi add indico --answer indico_event_ids='["<id>"]' or --answer indico_category_ids='["<id>"]' . Public events only. With no answer it reads the CERN workshop event 1716863. jira jira Archi reads a cache that a downloader writes, and archi add jira stops if the cache is missing. So download first: python -m archi.downloaders.jira --output-dir <data root>/jira --project <KEY> (repeat --project ; set CERN_JIRA_TOKEN in the environment if the projects are not public), then archi add jira . <data root> is the data_root: value in archi.yaml . The downloader needs the jira Python package ( pip install jira ). See python -m archi.downloaders.jira --help . Refreshing the cache is yours to schedule: the pack expects data no older than 24 hours, and archi doctor reports it when it is older. redmine tickets Like jira , Archi reads a cache that a downloader writes. Download first: python -m archi.downloaders.tickets --output-dir <data root>/tickets --redmine-url <url> (set REDMINE_API_KEY in the environment), then archi add tickets --answer tickets_base_url=<url> . The same pack reads JIRA Server or Data Center with --jira-url . See python -m archi.downloaders.tickets --help . Uploaded files, files copied into the data folder none No equivalent. Mattermost, Piazza, grader, Grafana service board none Not ported. See above. Adding a source says more about packs, and connector caches says what each downloader writes. The library lists every pack with its questions and credentials.
docs.title: Move each source

docs.text: Each stage has its own way back. v2 is never edited by the move, so the first two cost nothing. Abandon the 3.0 instance. v2 is untouched. From the instance directory: bash archi down --purge --yes # stops the stack and deletes its volumes cd ~ && rm -rf ~/archi3/$NAME3 Delete ~/.local/share/archi/$NAME3 too if you want the connector caches gone (that is the default data root). Pause a move. Run archi down (no --purge ). It keeps every volume. archi up brings the instance back with the same graph. Return your users to v2. If you pointed users or a proxy at 3.0, point them back. v2 never stopped. Restore v2 itself (only if v2 was damaged, for example after the cutover moved its branch). Use the v2 line, not 3.0. In a v2 environment: bash git checkout v2.5.0 # or the newest v2.x tag your site pinned pip install -e . archi delete -n $NAME # only if a broken deployment is still there archi create -n $NAME -c "$BK/deployment/<your config>.yaml" \ -e "$BK/deployment/<your secrets>.env" --services <your services> $RT exec -i postgres-$NAME pg_restore -U archi -d archi-db --clean --if-exists < "$BK/archi-db.dump" $RT run --rm -v archi-data-$NAME:/data -v "$BK":/backup alpine \ tar xzf /backup/archi-data.tgz -C /data The config and secrets are the files you used the first time. The copy of the deployment folder in the backup shows which they were. archi delete without --rmv keeps the volumes, and the restore then overwrites them.
docs.title: Roll back

docs.text: If you run a v2 deployment, tell the maintainers. The cutover waits until every live deployment has a named owner and has either moved or chosen to stay on a tagged v2.x release. A deployment that stays on v2 should pin the tag it runs, so a later fix on main cannot change it.

docs.text: The operations layer The operations layer runs automations over the context layer. It is the purpose of Archi 3.0. Agents propose. A separate component, the mediator , acts. No agent holds a credential that can change an external system. The loop Every automation follows the same loop. signal -> context read -> proposal -> decision -> action -> outcome Signal. A schedule fires, a ticket arrives or a watched value crosses a threshold. Context read. The runtime reads the graph at one pinned generation and checks the context gate . Proposal. The agent writes a typed proposal: a summary, the ids of the evidence it used, an action class and payload, a confidence and a rollback. Decision. The autonomy policy, and at L2 a person, decide. Action. The mediator carries out an approved action class. Outcome. The result is checked later and written to the ops-record . The loop runs as an OKG deployment workflow, scheduled by DBOS (a durable workflow library). Durable state lives in the database, never in a local file. Automation packs An automation pack declares one automation: a trigger : a schedule, a new ticket in a queue, or a watched signal a context gate a playbook : the instructions the agent follows action classes : each with a typed payload, its mediator, whether it is reversible, a blast-radius note and the highest level it may have a proposal schema and a budget (cost per run and per day, runs per hour) Tool packs ship the live tools that act as mediators. An automation never calls an external system any other way. See Writing an automation . Autonomy levels Level Meaning In 3.0 L0 observe Writes findings to the ops-record only. Yes L1 draft Drafts a reply or a ticket for a person to send. Yes L2 propose Proposes an action. It runs only after a person approves an escalation. A timed-out proposal never runs. Yes L3 act within limits Runs a reversible action without review, inside rate and budget limits. No Why not L3. There is no live track record of L2 automations yet. Without one, nobody can say that an automation is safe to run unreviewed. So the 3.0 runtime refuses an L3 setting wherever it appears: in a pack, a bundle, archi.yaml , or at run start. L3 is revisited once L2 automations have a live history. Three rules set the level: The instance sets each automation's level in its own archi.yaml . A bundle only sets an upper bound. The effective level is the lowest of the instance level, the bundle bound and the pack maximum. An action class has its own highest level too. # archi.yaml automations: instance-health: level: L1 Shadow and promotion Every automation starts in shadow at its configured level. It proposes and records, and nothing runs. Its proposals are scored against what people did on the same incidents: how often it agreed, how often it was wrong, how quickly it would have responded. Going live needs recorded shadow results and an operator's approval: archi ops promote <automation> The command refuses unless the shadow report passes the thresholds (by default at least 30 proposals, 20 answered, 50% coverage, 80% agreement and at most a 10% false-proposal rate; each can be changed with a flag). It then opens a change in the instance repository that holds the report. An operator approves that change with okg pact decide . Archi never takes that step. Until it is approved, the automation stays in shadow. Editing ops.yaml to say live changes nothing. An automation can go live with no shadow trial when someone decided so: archi ops promote <automation> --no-trial --note "<decision>" skips the thresholds and records the decision in the change. An operator still approves it. To go back, set mode: shadow for the automation in ops.yaml . From the next run on it sends nothing, and a run already waiting for an approval sends nothing either: the step that acts reads ops.yaml again. A live automation whose context gate fails runs in shadow for that run. It stays in shadow until a promotion is approved after the failure. Halt archi ops halt stops every automation on the instance. It pauses the scanner, rejects each open escalation, cancels runs that have not finished and records them as halted . archi ops resume undoes the pause. Halt wraps OKG's pause and drain until OKG ships a first-class kill switch. archi ops Command What it does archi ops status Levels, schedules, pending escalations, budgets and shadow scores. archi ops pending Escalations waiting for a person. archi ops approve <id> / reject <id> Decide an escalation. archi ops halt / resume Stop or restart all automations. archi ops promote <automation> Ask for an automation to go live. The full list is in the command reference . The details of the runtime (the worker, ops.yaml , the mediator contract, recovery after a crash) are in Running automations . What ships Two automation packs ship. ticket-triage , the reference automation in the design, triages new and updated Redmine, JIRA and ServiceNow tickets: a cited draft at L1, and at L2 an approved assignment, status change or posted reply (the reply written by a model when proposer.drafter is set). At SubMIT it replaces the v2 Redmine bot at the 3.0 cutover, with no shadow trial first (board d717). instance-health is an automation that watches the instance itself (doctor results, source freshness, failed ingests, automation error rates) and keeps one issue per problem in the instance repository. It starts at L1 and runs in shadow until promoted.

docs.text: Quickstart From an empty machine to a cited answer from your team's knowledge graph, with the cern-team bundle: five user commands, the same ones the nightly build runs (the cd is not counted, and the fifth is a check). You need: docker or podman (with compose ), Python 3.12 (CI tests 3.12; akmon 0.6.0 does not install on 3.14), and git . No account, key or root access. With rootless podman, container health checks run from systemd user timers. Where there is no systemd user session (inside a container, or on some shared hosts), the checks may never run, and then archi up waits with no time limit. Use docker there, or log in to a session with a systemd user manager. pip install archi-kb==3.0.2 archi init myteam --bundle cern-team cd myteam archi up archi doctor --json python "$ARCHI_CHECKOUT/python/tests/cli/mcp_cited_answer.py" "What is the Knowledge Bases and Agents for CERN workshop?" What each command does: Install. okg is the knowledge-graph engine; its PyPI package is akmon . archi-kb is Archi. The import name is archi . Both come from PyPI: installing archi-kb installs a matching akmon (0.6.x). Do not pip install archi : that name on PyPI is an unrelated package. Use a new virtual environment: one that still has the old okg package needs pip uninstall okg first, because both install the same files. archi init myteam --bundle cern-team creates ./myteam as a git repository. It writes the settings, generates every secret into .env , starts the graph database and publishes a first graph. The default packs need no credential. ( cd myteam then moves into it.) archi up starts the stack: graph database, chat database, MCP server and Open WebUI. It prints the chat address and the MCP endpoint. archi doctor --json runs every check and prints one JSON object. Each failure carries a fix line. Leave out --json for plain lines. The last command asks a question over MCP and succeeds only when the answer cites graph records. The script is in the Archi repository, so set ARCHI_CHECKOUT to a clone of this release ( git clone --branch v3.0.2 https://github.com/archi-physics/archi ). It needs the mcp Python package. In daily use you ask in the chat instead, or connect an agent . Check the result archi doctor exits 0 when no check failed. The last command prints the question, the record ids it cited and the source that wrote them. The nightly build runs these same commands on an empty runner and reports how long the whole path took (the target is 15 minutes). A test keeps this page and that build in step. Where next What each command does , including a local model and a remote host. Connect an agent such as Claude Code. Add a source . Operate the instance .

docs.text: Writing an automation An automation is an automation pack. It declares what starts a run, what context it needs, what the agent reads, and which actions it may propose. You write the declaration. The runtime runs it. Read the operations layer first. The full key list is in Automation packs . The shipped example is instance-health . Steps Make the pack. kind: automation , with requires.packs naming the packs whose live tools will carry out its actions, and ops-record so it can record what it does. Choose the trigger. One of: schedule with a cron of five fields ticket_queue with a system ( redmine , jira or servicenow ) and a queue signal with a source and a condition Archi refuses a cron that can fire more often than budget.runs_per_hour . 3. Set the context gate. Name the sources, the maximum staleness, the minimum context-eval score and the invariants that must hold. A gate must check something. If it fails, the run drops to shadow and says why. 4. Write the playbook. A Markdown file under the pack's playbooks/ directory. It is the instruction the agent follows. 5. Define the action classes. For each: a payload_schema (JSON Schema), a mediator , reversible , a blast_radius sentence and a max_level . The mediator is either a live tool ( archi.tools.x:fn ) or a workflow step. An action that changes an outside system must be a live tool. A live tool that can run at L2 must also be listed under idempotent_tools , so a retry has the effect once. 6. Fix the proposal schema. It must require summary , evidence_ids , action_class , payload , confidence and rollback . A proposal without evidence ids is invalid. 7. Set the budget and levels. cost_per_run , cost_per_day and runs_per_hour must be positive. default_level and max_level are L0 , L1 or L2 . L3 is refused. 8. Check it. bash archi bundles validate path/to/your-pack The command lists every problem in one run: a missing playbook, an action class that is not defined, a mediator that resolves to nothing, an invalid schema. Turn it on An instance selects the pack ( archi init --with or archi add ), sets the level in archi.yaml and names the automation in ops.yaml . See Running automations . Every automation starts in shadow. Promotion to live needs scored shadow results and an operator's approval. Rules to keep in mind Agents propose. Mediators act. Never give an agent a credential. Prefer a fixed check to an agent where one will do. Name the highest level honestly. L2 means a person approves every action.
docs.title: Writing an automation

docs.text: Bundles and packs in this release Each page below is generated from the manifest in the repository, so it cannot drift from what ships. Bundles Bundle Description cern-team A generic CERN team knowledge instance - documentation, meetings, wiki, documents, tickets and code. cluster-manager A cluster manager's knowledge instance - documentation, tickets, operational memory and, optionally, ServiceNow, Slurm, HTCondor, node health and code. cms-comp-ops A CMS computing operations knowledge instance - sites, storage, datasets and workflows from the CMS catalogs, site status, CMSSW releases, and the operational memory of past incidents. cms-physics A CMS physics knowledge instance - physics TWiki pages, CDS records, CMSSW releases, analysis notes, and the analysis ids, groups and techniques that link them. context CERN Document Server records, harvested over the public OAI-PMH endpoint. cms-analyses context CMS physics group and technique hubs, and rules joining analysis ids across CDS records, TWiki docs.text: Operating an instance An instance is a directory made by archi init . It is a git repository that holds configuration, never data or secrets in git. The day-to-day work is small: Task Command or page Is everything healthy? archi doctor . See Doctor . Start or stop the stack archi up , archi down . See Data persistence . Add a source archi add <pack> . See Adding a source . See what drifted from the install archi diff Check that the instance answers archi eval . See archi eval . Move to a newer Archi Upgrade and migration Run automations archi ops . See the operations layer . Something looks wrong Footgun ledger More detail on each command is in What each command does . The settings files are described in archi.yaml . What lives where archi.yaml : the instance's settings. archi.lock : which bundle and pack versions were installed. .env : the generated secrets and your source credentials, readable only by you, ignored by git. profiles/ , deployments/ : the rendered profile and the OKG deployment. The data root ( ~/.local/share/archi/<name> by default): connector caches and repository checkouts. It is outside the instance on purpose, because okg install --force deletes everything inside a deployment. OKG publishes only from a committed repository. Commit changes to archi.yaml and ops.yaml before the next publish.

docs.text: archi.yaml : the instance's settings. archi.lock : which bundle and pack versions were installed. .env : the generated secrets and your source credentials, readable only by you, ignored by git. profiles/ , deployments/ : the rendered profile and the OKG deployment. The data root ( ~/.local/share/archi/<name> by default): connector caches and repository checkouts. It is outside the instance on purpose, because okg install --force deletes everything inside a deployment. OKG publishes only from a committed repository. Commit changes to archi.yaml and ops.yaml before the next publish.
docs.title: What lives where

docs.text: What each command does The commands behind the quickstart , in more detail. All of them take --instance DIR (default: the current directory). The generated command reference lists every option. archi up prints the chat address, the admin account and the MCP endpoint. The passwords and the MCP bearer token are in myteam/.env . archi init <name> [--bundle B] [--with P] [--answer ID=VALUE] creates ./<name>/ as a git repository and commits a baseline. It renders the bundle into profiles/ , generates every secret into .env (mode 0600, git-ignored), and writes archi.yaml and compose.yaml . Then it starts the graph database and runs okg install , commits the deployment, publishes with okg provision , and sets okg's role passwords. Every path it passes to okg is absolute. The data root, where connector caches and repository checkouts go, is ~/.local/share/archi/<name> ( --data-root to change it) and must lie outside the instance. The default bundle is cern-team . Its default packs publish with no answer and no credential. docsite downloads two small public documentation sites (the FTS3 and Rucio docs) into its records cache before the first ingest; indico reads one public event, "Knowledge Bases and Agents for CERN", live. Read your own instead with --answer docsite_urls=<url>[,<url>...] and --answer indico_event_ids='["<id>"]' (or --answer indico_category_ids=... ). The public CMSSW release catalog is no longer a default; add it with --with cmssw-releases . If a documentation page cannot be fetched, init stops and names it. archi up starts one compose project, archi-<name> , on one network: Service What Published on graph-db AKMON Postgres, with okg's preload libraries 127.0.0.1, for okg on the host chat-db Open WebUI's own Postgres not published mcp okg mcp-serve , read-only, bearer token 127.0.0.1 webui Open WebUI v0.11.4 127.0.0.1 It then signs in to the site as its admin (creating the account on first start), points it at a local ollama if one answers on port 11434 ( --ollama-url for another), and runs okg chat sync , which registers the graph tools and the preset and proves both. In the chat, pick the preset named after the site: the graph tools are bound to it, not to the raw model. archi doctor [--json] runs okg deployment lint , okg doctor , a source-freshness check (each source's age from okg's watermarks against the max_staleness its pack declares), and one check for each quickstart trap archi absorbs, and prints a fix line for each failure. --json prints one object for agents. Exit code 0 means no check failed. archi eval [--bundle B] [--model M] [--model-url URL] [--out DIR] asks the bundle's smoke questions of the instance through its MCP endpoint, with a local model that can call tools, and writes report.md and report.json . It exits 1 below the bundle's pass threshold. Start ollama with OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=16384 or more first (see A local model ). See archi eval . archi down stops the project and keeps every volume. archi down --purge --yes also deletes the graph, chat and webui volumes; that is the reset (okg keeps its ownership claim in the database, so deleting the folder alone is not one). Your data persists across archi down and archi up (the published graph is the same generation), but not across --purge . An instance created before 2026-10-26 kept its graph only inside the container (the volume was mounted at the wrong path), so after upgrading archi, re-run archi init for it rather than archi up . Adding sources archi add <pack> --answer ID=VALUE adds a pack to a running instance and publishes again. See Adding a source . If the bundle names companions for that pack (cms-comp-ops: git-code brings code-text ), they come too and a note says so; --without <companion> leaves one out. archi ingest [--include SOURCE,...] [--publish] runs okg ingest for the instance from its directory, with the values in .env added to okg's environment (a value exported in the shell wins). That is how a source credential written into .env reaches the source. It is the fix archi doctor names for a stale source. --publish then publishes a new generation ( okg run --once --apply ). With an automation pack selected, both run in-process ( --inline ), because a queued ingest would run in the runtime worker, which does not read .env . It exits with okg's code. A local model The chat needs a model server. With ollama on the same machine, archi up finds it. Two things to know: Set the model at init: archi init myteam --answer chat_model=<a model ollama list shows> . The bundle default is llama3.1:8b . ollama's default context window (4096 tokens) is smaller than the preset's system prompt plus the graph tools' descriptions, so ollama cuts the prompt and the model never sees its tools. Start ollama with OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=16384 or more, or set num_ctx in the chat's controls. Any MCP client can use the graph without a model in the chat: point it at the MCP endpoint archi up printed, with OKG_CHAT_MCP_TOKEN from .env as the bearer token. A remote host Every port is bound to 127.0.0.1. On a remote machine, archi up prints the ssh -L command that tunnels the chat to your own browser. The long quickstart The older long cern-team quickstart is kept in the repository as reference material ( docs/cern-team-quickstart.md ). Each of its traps is listed in the footgun ledger , as absorbed by archi or filed with AKMON.
